content.value_statement: Weak domain layers scatter business rules and make validation inconsistent. This skill helps Claude, Codex, and Claude Code design expressive Rust domain models.
actual_capabilities: Identifies primitive obsession in Rust domain types.
Suggests value objects with validation constructors.
Moves business rules into entities and aggregates.
Models domain events for important state changes.
Highlights anemic domain models and service-heavy logic.
limitations: Focuses on Rust domain layer design, not database or UI code.
Provides patterns and examples, not complete application architecture.
Cannot prove business rules are correct without domain context.
Does not run tests or inspect files beyond allowed read tools.

use_cases.title: Refactor Primitive Models
use_cases.description: Convert string-heavy entities into validated value objects and clearer domain types.

use_cases.title: Design Business Rules
use_cases.description: Place validation, state changes, and invariants inside entities instead of services.

use_cases.title: Review Domain Architecture
use_cases.description: Check whether a Rust domain layer follows hexagonal architecture and domain-driven design principles.

prompt_templates.title: Find Domain Smells
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of an existing model.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this Rust domain model for primitive obsession and anemic design. Suggest the first three improvements.

prompt_templates.title: Create Value Objects
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me turn these domain fields into Rust value objects with validation, clear errors, and ergonomic constructors.

prompt_templates.title: Move Rules Into Entities
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced refactor from service logic to domain behavior.
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor this service-heavy workflow so the Rust entities own the state transitions and business invariants.

prompt_templates.title: Model Events and Aggregates
prompt_templates.prompt: Design aggregates and domain events for this Rust bounded context. Explain entity boundaries, invariants, and event publication points.

output_examples.input: A user model stores email, status, and age as plain strings and integers.
output_examples.output: The skill would recommend dedicated Email, UserStatus, and Age types with validation before entity construction.

output_examples.input: Order confirmation rules are implemented in an application service.
output_examples.output: The skill would move editable status checks and minimum order rules into the Order entity behavior.

output_examples.input: A team wants to publish domain events when users change email addresses.
output_examples.output: The skill would suggest recording an EmailChanged event inside the entity during the state transition.

best_practices: Provide real domain rules and examples before asking for a redesign.
Ask for small refactors first when a model has many responsibilities.
Review generated patterns against product language and business constraints.
anti_patterns: Do not ask it to design persistence models as if they were domain entities.
Do not accept generated business rules without stakeholder validation.
Do not mix infrastructure concerns into value object and entity design.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps design Rust domain models with validated types, entity behavior, domain events, and explicit business rules.

faq.question: Does it write complete Rust applications?
faq.answer: No. It focuses on domain layer structure and examples, not full application delivery.

faq.question: Can it review existing code?
faq.answer: Yes. It can inspect provided Rust models and suggest domain-driven improvements.

faq.question: Is this useful outside hexagonal architecture?
faq.answer: Yes. The value object and entity patterns apply to many Rust backend designs.

faq.question: Does it require external tools?
faq.answer: No. The skill only declares read and grep style access for reviewing text.

faq.question: Can it verify every business rule?
faq.answer: No. It needs domain experts to confirm rules, edge cases, and product language.
